# Learning Goals: Gamify Your In-Class Live Quiz

**Generated by:** Skill 02 — Learning Goals
**Workshop slug:** gamify_live_quiz
**Bloom's level:** Apply
**ARIVA format:** 10-minute workshop

---

## Intended Learning Outcome (ILO)

By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

> **Design** a single live-quiz question that connects a game mechanic to a specific learning outcome — so students retrieve and apply knowledge rather than guess.

---

## Why This ILO

"Apply" is the right Bloom's level here: participants are not just learning what gamification is — they are producing something (a question) that demonstrates they can use the principle. The workshop's Verarbeitung task makes this achievable in 10 minutes because it narrows the deliverable to *one question*, not a full quiz. Asking participants to design an entire gamified lesson would exceed both the time budget and the cognitive load appropriate for a first exposure.

---

## How the ILO Maps to ARIVA

| Phase | What it does for the ILO |
|---|---|
| **A — Arrival** | Announces the ILO directly — "by the end you'll be able to design one live-quiz question that actually checks learning" |
| **R — Reactivating** | Surfaces the participation gap they already experience — the problem the ILO solves |
| **I — Informing** | Delivers the core principle: game mechanic + learning outcome = effective live quiz |
| **V — Verarbeitung** | Participants apply the principle by writing one question tied to a real learning outcome from their own course |
| **A — Assessing** | Checks whether participants can articulate the difference between a retrieval question and a recognition/attention question |

---

## Assessing Question

The ILO is checked in the final 60 seconds with this question:

> "What's the difference between a quiz question that checks understanding and one that just checks whether students were paying attention?"

A participant has met the ILO if: they can articulate that a well-designed question requires active retrieval or application — not recognition of something stated seconds earlier, and not guessable from context or answer options alone.

---

## What This Workshop Does NOT Cover

To protect the 10-minute scope, the following are explicitly out of scope:

- Walkthroughs of specific tools (Kahoot!, Mentimeter, Poll Everywhere) — tool choice is secondary to question design
- Designing a multi-question quiz arc across a full lesson — that requires a separate session
- Grading, scoring models, or assessment validity — important but not the entry point
- Adapting gamification for online or asynchronous formats — a different design challenge

---

## Facilitator Note

In the Arrival phase, state the ILO as a concrete deliverable: *"By the end of this 10 minutes, you'll have written one live-quiz question that uses a game mechanic to check whether your students actually understood something — not just whether they were awake."* The specificity ("one question," "your students," "actually understood") sets the right expectation and pre-empts the common fear that gamification requires a complete course redesign.
